exercises.title: Architecture Documentation Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Learn architecture documentation vocabulary: 4+1 view model, logical vs. physical architecture, ADRs, arc42 template, deployment diagrams - the language of professional architecture documentation.

questions.q: The architect says: 'We follow the 4+1 view model for our architecture documentation.' What is the '4+1 view model'?
options: A model with four cloud regions plus one disaster recovery region
A framework describing software architecture through four views (logical, process, development, physical) plus use case scenarios
A four-layer network architecture plus one security layer
A documentation standard with four chapters and one appendix
questions.explanation: The 4+1 view model, introduced by Philippe Kruchten, describes software architecture through five views: Logical (functionality), Process (dynamic behaviour), Development (code organisation), Physical (deployment), and Scenarios (+1 use cases that tie the other views together). It is widely used in enterprise architecture documentation.

questions.q: The tech lead explains: 'The logical architecture shows the components and their relationships, while the physical architecture shows where they run.' What is the key difference?
options: Logical architecture uses UML; physical architecture uses Terraform
Logical architecture describes what the system does and how parts relate; physical architecture describes how and where it is deployed
Logical architecture is for developers; physical architecture is for network engineers only
Logical architecture documents APIs; physical architecture documents databases
questions.explanation: Logical architecture focuses on the conceptual structure - components, layers, modules, and their relationships - independent of infrastructure. Physical architecture (also called deployment architecture) shows where components actually run: which servers, containers, cloud regions, and networks. Both views are necessary for a complete architectural picture.

questions.q: A developer says: 'The architecture is documented in the ADR for this decision.' What is an ADR?
options: Automated Deployment Record
Architecture Decision Record
Advanced Design Review
Application Data Repository
questions.explanation: ADR stands for Architecture Decision Record. An ADR is a short document that captures a significant architectural decision, its context, the options considered, the chosen solution, and the rationale. ADRs are stored in the repository alongside the code (often in /docs/adr/) and provide a historical record of why the architecture looks the way it does.

questions.q: The architect recommends: 'We use the arc42 template for documenting our system.' What is arc42?
options: A cloud provider's architecture certification framework
A standardised template for documenting software architectures, with 12 sections covering context, constraints, building blocks, and deployment
A UML modelling tool for drawing sequence diagrams
A programming language for infrastructure-as-code
questions.explanation: arc42 is a pragmatic, structured template for documenting software architectures. It organises documentation into 12 sections, including system context, constraints, solution strategy, building block view, runtime view, deployment view, and architectural decisions. It is widely adopted in German-speaking countries and increasingly used internationally.

questions.q: During a review, the engineer says: 'The deployment diagram shows we have two app servers behind a load balancer with a shared database.' What does a deployment diagram show?
options: The sequence of API calls during user login
The physical or virtual infrastructure: nodes, servers, containers, networks, and how software components are distributed across them
The database schema and entity relationships
The CI/CD pipeline stages from build to production
questions.explanation: A deployment diagram (a UML artefact, also Level 4 in C4 model terms) shows the physical or virtual infrastructure: nodes (servers, VMs, containers, devices), communication paths (networks, protocols), and which software components are deployed on which nodes. It is essential for understanding availability, scaling, and infrastructure dependencies.

questions.q: PR Description: "Fix: Updated API endpoint to handle user authentication. This change utilizes the new OAuth2 flow as outlined in the architecture document. The previous implementation was vulnerable to brute-force attacks due to a lack of rate limiting."
options: The PR description is unnecessarily verbose and should focus solely on the code changes made.

The PR description accurately reflects the architectural context of the change, referencing the relevant documentation and highlighting security considerations. This demonstrates an understanding of how individual code contributions fit into the broader system design .
The phrase 'as outlined in the architecture document' is vague and should be replaced with a specific reference to the diagram or component definition.
Rate limiting is irrelevant to OAuth2 authentication, and the PR description should focus on the OAuth2 flow itself.
questions.explanation: This question assesses understanding of how architecture documentation informs development work. The correct answer emphasizes that a good PR description connects the code change to its architectural context - in this case, referencing the document and highlighting security implications. It corrects the misconception that PR descriptions should only detail code modifications; integrating architectural considerations is crucial for maintainability and consistency.

questions.q: Sarah : "Hey team, I'm working on the new microservice for order processing. The architecture document mentions a 'bounded context' for orders. Can someone explain what that means in practice? It seems like just another buzzword."
options: insufficient - the bounded context is simply a naming convention.
correct - a bounded context defines a self-contained area of responsibility within the system, focusing on a specific domain and its related data.
incorrect - a bounded context refers to the physical location where the service is deployed, ensuring isolation.
incorrect - it's a technical term for the number of API calls made per second by the service.
questions.explanation: Bounded contexts are a crucial architectural concept that helps manage complexity in microservices. Essentially, each bounded context represents a single business domain with its own data model and logic, minimizing dependencies between services. This contrasts with having a monolithic database containing all order-related information, which would be prone to conflicts and difficult to evolve independently - the key is clear boundaries around responsibility.

questions.q: David asks during a code review: "The architecture document mentions 'domain model'. What does that specifically refer to in this context - is it just the data structure or something more?" Consider the following options for responding to David .
options: Insufficient - the domain model only describes the data entities involved.

Correct - the domain model represents the core business concepts and rules of the system, including their relationships and constraints. It's more than just a data structure; it's the conceptual representation of how the business operates.
The domain model is simply a synonym for 'data model', focusing on the tables and columns within the database schema.
Correct - the domain model is a high-level abstraction that focuses solely on the data structures used to represent information, ignoring any business logic or rules.
questions.explanation: David 's question highlights a common misunderstanding of 'domain model'. It's not *just* about the database schema (option A); it represents the core business concepts and their relationships. The domain model captures the 'what' of the business - the rules and processes - rather than merely the 'how' represented by the data structure (options C & D). Option B is a more accurate description, emphasizing the conceptual nature of the model.

exercises.title: C4 Model Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practice C4 model diagram vocabulary: Context (L1), Container (L2), Component (L3), and Code (L4) diagrams, zoom in/out language, and describing system boundaries.

questions.q: In the C4 model, what does a Level 1 (Context) diagram show?
options: The internal classes of a single component
The high-level view of the system and how it interacts with users and other systems - without any implementation detail
The database schema
The deployment environment
questions.explanation: A C4 Level 1 (Context) diagram is the highest-level view - it shows your system as a single box, surrounded by the people and other systems that interact with it. It answers: 'What does this system do and who uses it?'

questions.q: A C4 Level 2 (Container) diagram shows which level of detail?
options: Individual classes and functions
The major deployable units inside the system - web apps, APIs, databases, message queues - and how they communicate
The physical servers
The team structure
questions.explanation: A C4 Container diagram zooms into the system to show the major technical containers: web frontend, backend API, database, message broker, etc. 'Container' here means a deployable/runnable unit - not necessarily Docker.

questions.q: When would you use a C4 Level 3 (Component) diagram?
options: To show the entire company's IT landscape
To zoom into a specific container and show its major internal components and their responsibilities
To document every function in the codebase
To show infrastructure networking
questions.explanation: A C4 Component diagram zooms into a specific container (e.g., the backend API) to show its internal components - controllers, services, repositories - and how they interact. Use it when you need to explain a container's internal architecture.

questions.q: What does 'zoom in / zoom out' mean when presenting C4 diagrams?
options: Changing the zoom level in your diagramming tool
Moving between C4 levels to add or remove detail - zooming in goes from Context → Container → Component, zooming out goes the other way
Resizing the diagram window
Changing font size
questions.explanation: 'Zoom in / zoom out' is the C4 model's key navigation metaphor. You start at Context (big picture), zoom in to Containers (technical architecture), then Components (internal design). This lets you explain a system at any audience's level of detail.

questions.q: How would you describe a 'boundary' in a C4 Context diagram?
options: A physical fence around the data center
The border of your system - everything inside the boundary is your system's responsibility; everything outside is an external person or system
A network firewall rule
A database transaction boundary
questions.explanation: In C4, a boundary (shown as a dashed box) separates your system from external actors. When presenting, you might say: 'Inside this boundary is our payment system. Outside, we have the customer's browser, the bank API, and the fraud detection service.'

questions.q: Sarah : "Hey team, I'm working on the new payment processing API. I've created a Level 2 diagram showing the User, Payment Service, and Database containers. It's pretty detailed - I can see all the interactions between them. Should I share this with the wider team?"
options: insufficient - the diagram only shows the technical architecture, not the business value.
appropriate - Level 2 diagrams are standard for documenting APIs and clearly illustrate dependencies.
potentially problematic - Level 2 diagrams can be overwhelming for stakeholders unfamiliar with the system. Consider a simpler view first.
incorrect - Level 2 diagrams should always include user flows to fully represent the system's functionality.
questions.explanation: Sarah is using correct terminology when discussing C4 Level 2 diagrams. These diagrams are designed for detailed documentation of containers and their interactions, which is exactly what she's doing by showcasing the User, Payment Service, and Database. The other options misinterpret the purpose or level of detail associated with a Level 2 diagram - it's about technical dependencies, not necessarily business value or user flows at this stage.

questions.q: John : 'I'm reviewing this PR for the new user onboarding flow. The developer used a Level 2 diagram in the PR description to show the User, Authentication, and Profile containers. It includes a lot of detail about the data passed between them - specifically, the user_id being serialized as JSON. I'm not sure if this is *too* granular for a simple feature change.' Which of the following best describes John's concern?
options: It indicates a clear understanding of data serialization techniques, which is excellent.
It suggests the developer prioritized technical accuracy over overall clarity and potential complexity.
The Level 2 diagram is unnecessary for a small PR and should be simplified.
The inclusion of user_id in the JSON details demonstrates proper security practices.
questions.explanation: John's concern stems from the idea that excessive detail in a C4 diagram, particularly at Level 2, can obscure the *purpose* of the PR. While technical accuracy is important, a Level 2 diagram should primarily illustrate the container relationships and their interactions, not every data point exchanged. Over-detailing like this can make it harder for reviewers to quickly grasp the core change being implemented - a key principle of effective C4 diagrams.

questions.q: David : "I'm creating a PR to add support for two-factor authentication. I've included a Level 2 C4 diagram showing the User, Authentication Service, and Identity Provider containers. It details the flow of tokens and passwords being exchanged. Is this level of detail appropriate for this change?"
options: insufficient - the PR only addresses token exchange.
appropriate - it clearly illustrates the authentication workflow.
incorrect - Level 2 diagrams should only show high-level container interactions.
redundant - a Level 1 diagram would have been sufficient to describe the authentication flow.
questions.explanation: David's situation highlights a key use case for Level 2 C4 diagrams: illustrating complex workflows . While Level 1 diagrams show broad context, Level 2 diagrams allow you to delve into the interactions between containers, which is exactly what's needed when describing a feature like two-factor authentication. The inclusion of token exchange details demonstrates an understanding of the underlying system - it's appropriate for this level of change.

questions.q: Alex : 'I'm writing the PR description for this new microservice. I've used a C4 Level 2 diagram to illustrate the interaction between the `Order Service` and the `Payment Gateway`. It shows how the service calls the gateway API, handles responses, and manages transaction IDs. Should I include specifics about the HTTP methods (GET, POST) used in the description?'
options: insufficient - the diagram only illustrates high-level relationships.
correct - including HTTP method details ensures clarity for developers unfamiliar with the service.
excessive - focusing on API calls obscures the overall business logic of the microservice.
necessary - documenting every detail is crucial for future maintainability and debugging.
questions.explanation: The question tests understanding of when to include specific technical details in a C4 diagram's documentation. While including method details like GET or POST can be helpful, the core purpose of a Level 2 diagram is to show container interactions. Focusing solely on these granular elements risks losing sight of the larger system architecture and business process that the diagram represents-the primary goal is still high-level relationship visualization. Including HTTP methods should be reserved for more detailed documentation or specific use cases where it's crucial.

questions.q: PR Description During a code review, Liam comments on a PR describing a new feature: 'I've used a C4 Level 2 diagram to illustrate the flow between the `User` and `Notification Service` containers. It shows how the service sends push notifications based on user events.' His colleague, Maya, responds with: 'That's great context! But is Level 2 really necessary here? Shouldn't we focus on the high-level interaction - sending a notification when an event occurs - rather than detailing the specific message format and queue names?'
options: Insufficient - the diagram lacks details about error handling.
Correct - Level 2 diagrams are always appropriate for describing complex interactions.
Incorrect - using Level 2 is overkill; a Level 1 diagram would have sufficed to explain the overall flow.
Incorrect - focusing solely on the high-level interaction obscures potential technical complexities that could impact future development.
questions.explanation: The correct answer highlights Maya's astute observation. Level 2 diagrams are powerful but can quickly become overly detailed, obscuring the core purpose of the C4 model which is to provide strategic context. While a Level 2 diagram *can* be useful for illustrating complex interactions, in this scenario, focusing on the high-level flow - 'sending a notification when an event occurs' - is sufficient and aligns better with the goal of communicating the feature's intent without getting bogged down in implementation details. Options A and B are incorrect because error handling isn't always relevant to the initial context, and Level 2 diagrams *are* appropriate for complex interactions.

exercises.title: Cloud Infrastructure Diagram Language
exercises.subtitle: Practice describing AWS, Azure, and GCP architecture diagrams in English.

questions.q: An AWS diagram shows an EC2 instance inside a private subnet inside a VPC. How would you describe this?
options: The EC2 instance is on the internet.
The EC2 instance is in a private subnet within a VPC, isolated from direct internet access.
The VPC is inside the EC2 instance.
The subnet is the server.
questions.explanation: Private subnets within a VPC isolate resources from the internet. EC2 instances in private subnets require a NAT gateway for outbound traffic.

questions.q: A diagram shows an Application Load Balancer distributing traffic to an Auto Scaling Group. What does this describe?
options: A single EC2 instance handling all traffic.
Elastic compute capacity: the ALB distributes incoming requests across dynamically scaled EC2 instances.
A database cluster.
A static website deployment.
questions.explanation: ALB + Auto Scaling Group is the standard pattern for horizontally scalable, highly available web application deployments on AWS.

questions.q: A GCP diagram shows Cloud Armor in front of a Cloud Load Balancer. What is Cloud Armor's role?
options: Cloud Armor is the application server.
Cloud Armor provides WAF and DDoS protection at the edge, filtering malicious traffic before it reaches the load balancer.
Cloud Armor is a database.
Cloud Armor replaces the load balancer.
questions.explanation: Cloud Armor is GCP's web application firewall and DDoS protection service, positioned at the network edge.

questions.q: An Azure diagram shows a Resource Group containing a VNET, an App Service Plan, and Azure SQL. What does this imply?
options: These resources are in different subscriptions.
These Azure resources are logically grouped for lifecycle management and access control within a single resource group.
The resource group is a physical server.
App Service Plan contains Azure SQL.
questions.explanation: Azure Resource Groups are logical containers for organizing related resources with shared lifecycle, billing, and access policies.

questions.q: A diagram shows a multi-region deployment with Route 53 latency-based routing. What problem does this solve?
options: It reduces the number of servers needed.
It routes each user to the geographically nearest healthy region, minimizing latency and providing failover if one region goes down.
It increases database cost.
It removes the need for load balancing.
questions.explanation: Latency-based routing directs traffic to the closest region. Multi-region deployments provide both low latency and disaster recovery capability.

questions.q: Reviewer: 'I'm seeing this Azure diagram. We have a Function App deployed to a Consumption plan, and it's fronted by an Application Gateway. The diagram labels the Function App as having 'managed identities'. What does that mean in the context of this deployment?'
options: The Function App is automatically billed per execution, regardless of usage.
The Function App uses Azure Active Directory for authentication and authorization, simplifying access to other Azure resources without managing secrets directly.
Managed identities allow the Function App to securely access storage accounts without needing to store credentials in code or configuration files.
This indicates that the Function App is running on a dedicated virtual machine within the Application Gateway's network.
questions.explanation: Managed identities are a key feature for simplifying security. They allow Azure resources, like your Function App, to automatically authenticate with other Azure services (like storage accounts) without needing to store or manage credentials manually. This significantly reduces the risk of exposing secrets and streamlines the deployment process. Option A is incorrect because Consumption plans *are* billed per execution; option D describes a different architecture altogether.

questions.q: Reviewer: 'Hey team, I've reviewed this diagram of the new microservice architecture. We're using a Kubernetes cluster managed by EKS, and one of the services is deployed to a separate node group with a specific security policy applied via Network Policies. The diagram labels this node group as having 'Pod Security Admission'. Can someone explain what Pod Security Admission does here?', (Slack message)
options: It's a type of load balancer that distributes traffic to the pods within the node group.
It's a tool for monitoring the resource utilization of each pod running on the node group, ensuring optimal performance.
It enforces security policies at the pod level, controlling access to resources and preventing unauthorized actions like privileged containers or host network access.
It's a mechanism for automatically scaling the number of pods in the node group based on traffic demand.
questions.explanation: Pod Security Admission (PSA) is a critical component for securing Kubernetes deployments. Incorrectly assuming it's a load balancer or scaling tool misunderstands its core function. PSA defines and enforces policies that restrict what containers can do-specifically preventing insecure practices like running privileged containers or exposing the host network, which are common vulnerabilities. This ensures your microservices operate safely within the cluster.

questions.q: PR Description: 'Reviewers, I've updated the deployment diagram to reflect our new architecture. We're using a CloudFront distribution for static assets and an API Gateway to handle all incoming requests. The diagram labels the API Gateway as having 'origin shield' enabled. Can someone explain what origin shield does in this context and why it was chosen? It seems like a lot of overhead, but I want to ensure we're optimizing performance for our user base.
options: Origin Shield automatically caches all API responses, reducing load on the backend services.
Origin Shield provides DDoS protection by filtering malicious traffic before it reaches the API Gateway.
Origin Shield intelligently routes requests based on geographic location and network conditions to minimize latency.
Origin Shield is a deprecated feature that has been replaced with more advanced caching mechanisms.
questions.explanation: The correct answer, Origin Shield, provides DDoS protection by filtering malicious traffic *before* it reaches the API Gateway. This is its primary function and why it's beneficial in this scenario - mitigating potential attacks. The other options misrepresent Origin Shield's role; caching (option 1) isn't its core purpose, and geographic routing (option 3) is handled by other services like CloudFront or API Gateways themselves. It's important to understand that origin shield adds a layer of security without significantly impacting performance due to its efficient filtering mechanism.

exercises.title: Infrastructure Diagram Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practice infrastructure diagram vocabulary: VPC, subnets, availability zones, traffic flow descriptions, load balancer conventions, and firewall boundary language.

questions.q: In an infrastructure diagram, how would you describe the relationship between a VPC and a subnet?
options: They are the same thing
A VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) is the top-level isolated network; subnets are subdivisions of the VPC's IP range, typically separated into public and private tiers
A subnet is larger than a VPC
VPCs are for databases, subnets are for applications
questions.explanation: A VPC is your isolated virtual network with its own IP address range (CIDR block). Subnets are subdivisions of that range - public subnets have internet gateway access, private subnets don't. In diagrams, you show subnets as boxes inside the VPC box.

questions.q: When describing traffic flow in an infrastructure diagram, which phrase is standard?
options: The internet goes to the server
Traffic flows from the internet through the load balancer to the application tier in the private subnet
Data moves everywhere
Requests happen to the backend
questions.explanation: 'Traffic flows from X to Y' is the standard language. For infrastructure reviews you might say: 'Traffic flows from the internet through the WAF and ALB to the app servers in the private subnet, which then query the RDS instance in the database subnet.'

questions.q: What does 'availability zone' represent in an infrastructure diagram?
options: A time zone for scheduling deployments
An isolated data center location within a cloud region - resources spread across AZs survive a single AZ failure
A zone where the service is available to users
A firewall security zone
questions.explanation: An availability zone (AZ) is a physically separate data center within a cloud region. Infrastructure diagrams typically show resources replicated across 2-3 AZs with dashed or colored boxes separating them, to illustrate high-availability design.

questions.q: In an infrastructure diagram, what does a 'firewall boundary' typically represent visually?
options: A physical wall around the data center
A dashed or colored border showing where traffic is inspected/filtered - separating trusted from untrusted zones
A red line indicating danger
A dotted line showing data replication
questions.explanation: A firewall boundary in infrastructure diagrams is shown as a dashed box or colored border separating network security zones. Traffic crossing the boundary implies filtering or inspection rules. You'd say: 'All traffic crossing this boundary is inspected by the WAF.'

questions.q: How would you describe a load balancer's role when presenting an infrastructure diagram?
options: It makes the servers heavier
The load balancer sits between the internet and the application tier, distributing incoming requests across multiple instances to ensure availability and scalability
It balances the electrical load in the data center
It stores frequently accessed data
questions.explanation: When presenting, describe the load balancer's function: 'The Application Load Balancer receives all inbound HTTPS traffic and distributes it across the three app server instances in our autoscaling group, with health checks ensuring unhealthy instances are removed automatically.'

questions.q: During a code review of a new microservice deployment, your team lead asks you to clarify the diagram showing the network topology. He points out a specific instance of an internal load balancer and asks how it relates to the security group attached to the backend service instances. Which phrase best describes this relationship?
options: The load balancer acts as a direct firewall, enforcing all inbound rules.
The security group controls access *to* the load balancer, while the load balancer manages traffic *from* it.
The load balancer and security group are entirely separate entities with no interaction; the diagram is misleading.
The load balancer's configuration mirrors the security group settings for simplified management.
questions.explanation: Security groups control inbound/outbound traffic at the instance level, while a load balancer manages traffic distribution. The load balancer doesn't inherently act as a firewall; that function is typically handled by Network ACLs or the security group itself. Therefore, the security group controls access *to* the load balancer, and the load balancer manages traffic *from* it - this describes the standard operational relationship.

questions.q: During a design review for a new serverless API gateway, you're discussing the diagram with your team. A junior developer uses the term "transit routing" to describe how requests flow through the various components - from the client, via API Gateway, to the backend Lambda functions. You notice some confusion and want to provide a more precise explanation. Which phrase best clarifies the actual mechanism depicted in the diagram?
options: The API Gateway is acting as a simple switch, directing traffic based on URL paths.
Transit routing refers to the physical cables connecting the servers within the data center.
It describes the process where requests are dynamically routed between different backend services based on load and health.
Transit routing simply means that all incoming requests are processed sequentially through each stage of the API pipeline.
questions.explanation: The term "transit routing" is often used informally but doesn't accurately represent how modern API gateways operate. The diagram likely shows a dynamic routing process - where the gateway intelligently directs traffic based on factors like server load or health checks, rather than a simple sequential flow. This allows for scalability and fault tolerance; option 2 is a common misunderstanding of the term.

questions.q: During a standup meeting, you're presenting the updated infrastructure diagram for the new image processing service. A senior engineer asks: 'Can you explain how the data flows from the S3 bucket to the worker instances via the API Gateway? I'm seeing multiple routing configurations.' Which phrase accurately describes the primary mechanism illustrated by the diagram?
options: "The API Gateway acts as a single point of entry, directing all requests directly to the worker instances."
"Data is routed through a series of internal load balancers before reaching the worker instances, ensuring high availability and failover."
"The API Gateway leverages transit routing to dynamically route requests based on request headers and payload content, optimizing for performance."
"All data flows sequentially through the API Gateway, with no intermediate routing steps - this simplifies monitoring and troubleshooting."
questions.explanation: This scenario focuses on understanding dynamic routing. While the API Gateway *does* act as an entry point, the diagram illustrates a more nuanced approach: transit routing. This allows for intelligent traffic management based on request characteristics - crucial for services like image processing where different requests might require different worker instances or configurations. Option A is too simplistic; B accurately reflects the dynamic nature of transit routing; and C & D misrepresent the workflow.

questions.q: You're reviewing a PR for deploying a new database service. The diagram shows the service connected to an AWS Direct Connect gateway. During the review, a teammate asks: 'How does the Direct Connect connection impact the latency of queries against our PostgreSQL instance?' Which phrase accurately describes the key effect illustrated in the diagram?
options: The Direct Connect provides a dedicated, low-latency path for all network traffic, bypassing the public internet entirely.
The Direct Connect acts as a VPN tunnel, encrypting all data transmitted between the database and the application servers to ensure security.
The Direct Connect establishes a redundant connection, automatically switching over in case of failure to maintain service availability.
The Direct Connect provides a private connection for outbound traffic only, impacting inbound connections through the firewall.
questions.explanation: A Direct Connect gateway creates a dedicated network connection between your on-premises environment and AWS. This significantly reduces latency compared to routing traffic over the public internet, as it bypasses the complexities and potential congestion of standard internet routes. The key effect is a lower ping time for database queries, improving response times and overall application performance. Options B, C, and D misrepresent the primary function of a Direct Connect connection.

exercises.subtitle: Practice narrating microservices architecture diagrams in English for design reviews and interviews.

questions.q: How would you describe an API Gateway in a microservices diagram?
options: The API Gateway is just a proxy.
The API Gateway is the single entry point for all client requests, routing them to the appropriate downstream microservice.
The API Gateway is the database.
The API Gateway is optional.
questions.explanation: The API Gateway acts as a reverse proxy, handling routing, authentication, rate limiting, and other cross-cutting concerns.

questions.q: A diagram shows a message queue between Service A and Service B with a dashed arrow. What does this indicate?
options: Service A calls Service B synchronously.
Service A publishes messages to a queue which Service B consumes asynchronously.
The services share memory.
The dashed arrow means the connection is broken.
questions.explanation: Dashed arrows typically indicate asynchronous messaging. A queue between services shows decoupled, event-driven communication.

questions.q: You see a shared database icon connected to three services in a diagram. Why is this a common architecture concern?
options: Shared databases are the best practice for microservices.
A shared database creates tight coupling between services and makes independent deployment difficult.
The database icon should be colored red.
Three services sharing a database is always optimal.
questions.explanation: The shared database anti-pattern in microservices creates coupling because schema changes in one service affect all others.

questions.q: You need to describe horizontal scaling in a diagram where three identical service instances are shown. What do you say?
options: There are three different services.
The diagram shows three horizontally scaled instances of the same service behind a load balancer.
The service has three bugs.
The architecture is vertically scaled.
questions.explanation: Multiple identical instances behind a load balancer represent horizontal scaling - adding capacity by running more instances.

questions.q: A system design diagram shows a CDN at the edge before the load balancer. What is its purpose?
options: The CDN processes business logic.
The CDN caches static assets at edge locations geographically close to users, reducing origin server load.
The CDN replaces the database.
The CDN is for security only.
questions.explanation: CDNs cache and serve static content from edge nodes near users, reducing latency and load on origin infrastructure.

questions.q: Sarah : "Hey team, I've been reviewing this PR for the Order Service. It seems like we're directly calling a database function from within the service - should we be using an API to abstract that away?"
options: Insufficient - direct database calls are often the simplest and most performant solution.
Correct - exposing internal database logic through an API Gateway promotes loose coupling, improved testability, and easier future changes without impacting service code.
Neutral - direct database calls are acceptable as long as they're optimized for performance within the Order Service.
Incorrect - using a dedicated API Gateway adds unnecessary overhead and complexity to this simple operation.
questions.explanation: This scenario highlights the importance of API Gateways in microservices. The correct answer reflects the core benefit: decoupling the Order Service from the database logic by exposing it as an API. This avoids tight coupling, allowing for independent scaling and future modifications without requiring changes to the service itself. Options A, C, and D misrepresent the value proposition of API Gateways - they aren't just about adding complexity; they're about flexibility and maintainability.

questions.q: PR Description: "Implemented a new feature to calculate shipping costs. Directly calls `calculate_shipping()` function on the `OrderDB` object. This is faster than using an API."
options: insufficient - the PR lacks context regarding potential future changes and scalability concerns.
correct - direct database access improves performance, which is often a priority in development.
incorrect - abstracting database calls into APIs promotes loose coupling and easier maintenance over time.
incorrect - the PR description should primarily focus on the feature's functionality, not technical implementation details.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of architectural considerations beyond immediate performance. While faster access is tempting, directly calling database functions violates microservices principles by creating tight coupling and hindering independent scaling or technology changes in the future. A good PR description should acknowledge this risk and suggest a more flexible approach like exposing the functionality as an API, even if it initially introduces a small performance overhead. PR Descriptions should focus on *what* the code does, not *how*.

questions.q: Mark : "Just finished implementing the Payment Service. I've wrapped the entire payment processing logic in a single function called `process_payment()`. It's quick and easy!" As a senior developer during a code review, how would you respond to Mark 's statement regarding tight coupling within the service? Consider the potential impact on maintainability and resilience.
options: insufficient - the function is short and simple...
incorrect - it's best practice to always encapsulate all business logic in a single function for performance reasons.
correct - this approach creates tight coupling, making the service difficult to test, modify, and potentially leading to cascading failures if payment processing errors occur.
unacceptable - using a single function exposes sensitive payment data directly and violates security best practices.
questions.explanation: Mark 's statement highlights a common pitfall in microservices development: tightly coupled logic. While performance is important, bundling all payment processing into one function sacrifices modularity and testability. This creates dependencies between the service and its underlying implementation, making it harder to change or debug if problems arise - a key concern when designing resilient services. The correct option emphasizes the importance of separation of concerns and independent deployability that are core principles of microservices architecture.

questions.q: During a code review of the User Service PR, David says: 'I've directly injected the authentication logic into this service. It's the simplest way to handle it and avoids unnecessary network calls.' As a senior developer, what is your primary concern regarding David's approach? Consider potential risks to operational stability and future development effort.
options: Insufficient - direct database access is perfectly acceptable for performance-critical operations in microservices.
Insufficient - tightly coupled services are inherently more resilient due to reduced dependencies.
Potentially insufficient - injecting authentication logic directly introduces a single point of failure and makes future changes, like switching authentication providers, significantly more complex.
Correct - direct access is the optimal solution as it minimizes latency and avoids unnecessary communication overhead.
questions.explanation: David's statement highlights a critical concern: tight coupling. Injecting authentication logic directly into the User Service creates a dependency on that specific implementation, making future changes difficult and potentially introducing bugs. While minimizing network calls can be beneficial, it shouldn't come at the expense of maintainability and resilience - a key principle of microservices. Option B is partially correct but doesn't address the core issue of tight coupling.

questions.q: During a code review of the Product Service PR, Emily states: 'I've created a dedicated service for managing product inventory. It directly interacts with our core database to update stock levels whenever a sale occurs.' As a senior developer, which of the following best describes your immediate concern regarding this approach? Consider potential risks related to data consistency and system complexity.
options: Insufficient - direct database access is always the most efficient solution for critical operations.

Potentially problematic - introducing tight coupling between services can significantly increase the risk of cascading failures and complicate future updates. Consider implementing a well-defined event-driven architecture instead.

questions.explanation: This question assesses understanding of loose coupling in microservices. Options A is overly simplistic, B correctly identifies the core concern - dependency on a single service's database operations - while C downplays a significant risk and D promotes an anti-pattern for microservices architecture.

questions.q: In a sequence diagram, what is a 'lifeline'?
options: The total time the system has been running
A vertical dashed line below each participant that represents its existence over time in the interaction
A measurement of system uptime
The duration of a synchronous call
questions.explanation: A lifeline is the vertical dashed line that extends downward from each participant (actor or system) in a sequence diagram. It represents the participant's existence during the interaction. Activation boxes on the lifeline show when it's actively processing.

questions.q: What is the difference between a synchronous and asynchronous call in a sequence diagram?
options: Synchronous calls are faster
Synchronous calls (solid arrowhead) wait for a response before continuing; asynchronous calls (open arrowhead) send the message and continue without waiting
Synchronous calls go left to right, asynchronous go right to left
There is no difference in UML notation
questions.explanation: Synchronous calls use a solid filled arrowhead - the caller waits for a response. Asynchronous calls use an open (stick) arrowhead - the caller sends the message and immediately continues without waiting for a response.

questions.q: What does the 'alt' combined fragment represent in a sequence diagram?
options: An alternative system architecture
A conditional branch - like an if/else - showing different interaction paths based on a condition
An alternate diagram style
A deprecated UML notation
questions.explanation: The 'alt' (alternative) combined fragment represents conditional branching. It's the UML equivalent of if/else - you divide the fragment into guards (conditions), and only the path whose guard is true executes. Example: [user authenticated] vs. [user not authenticated].

questions.q: When would you use a 'loop' combined fragment in a sequence diagram?
options: When the system is running in circles
To show that a sequence of messages repeats a specified number of times or while a condition holds
When two systems communicate back and forth
To show a recursive function call
questions.explanation: The 'loop' fragment shows repetition - the contained interaction repeats while its guard condition is true, or for a specified number of iterations. Example: 'loop [for each order item] - call inventory check service.'

questions.q: What does a 'return message' look like in a sequence diagram and what does it represent?
options: A solid arrow going forward
A dashed arrow going back to the caller, representing the response returned from a synchronous call
A bold arrow going to the right
A dotted box around the caller
questions.explanation: A return message is shown as a dashed arrow pointing back to the caller. It represents the response from a synchronous call - e.g., 'HTTP 200 OK with order data.' Return messages are optional but help make the flow explicit.

A detailed explanation of the API endpoint's input parameters.
The sequence of messages exchanged between the client and the server during user login, showcasing the flow of data and control.
A list of all the security vulnerabilities addressed in the new authentication system.
questions.explanation: Sarah is using a sequence diagram to visualize the interaction. The diagram shows the order of messages - requests and responses - between the client (e.g., a web browser) and the server during user login. Options A and D are incorrect because they describe database details or security considerations, not the *flow* of the communication itself. Option B is also partially correct but misses the core purpose: sequence diagrams focus on *how* data moves, not just what parameters are involved.

The diagram highlights a potential performance issue due to synchronous communication and suggests an alternative design choice.

questions.q: A request arrives at the top of the diagram and flows down to the database. How would you describe this?

The request flows from top to bottom: from the client through the API gateway to the database.
The request is horizontal.
The diagram has no direction.
questions.explanation: Top-to-bottom flow is a common pattern in architecture diagrams representing request lifecycle from user to data store.

questions.q: In a C4 diagram, you are describing the boundary box labeled Payment Service. Which sentence is most precise?
options: The Payment Service is a thing.
The Payment Service container encapsulates all payment processing logic and communicates with the external Stripe API.
The box says payment.
The Payment Service is outside the system.
questions.explanation: C4 model container descriptions should name the software element, its responsibility, and its external relationships.

questions.q: Two services are connected by a solid arrow labeled REST/JSON. What does this communicate?
options: The services share a database.
Service A calls Service B synchronously using a REST API with JSON payloads.
The services are deployed together.
The arrow means they are unrelated.
questions.explanation: A labeled directed arrow in an architecture diagram shows the communication protocol and direction of the relationship.

questions.q: A component sits outside the main system boundary box. How would you describe this in a diagram walkthrough?
options: That component is internal to our system.
That component is an external system or third-party dependency outside our system boundary.
That component is not important.
That component is the database.
questions.explanation: In C4 and other architecture notations, elements outside the system boundary are external systems or third-party services.

questions.q: You are narrating a sequence diagram. An actor on the left sends a message to a box on the right. What do you say?
options: Something happened.
The user sends a POST /order request to the Order Service, which then queries the Inventory Service.
The box receives the actor.
The sequence is unclear.
questions.explanation: Sequence diagram narration specifies who initiates the interaction, what operation is performed, and what happens next.

The description suggests Sarah performed a technical debugging session, implying a deeper investigation than was actually done.
The description is too vague and doesn't clearly state the impact of the fix - it only describes the action taken.
The description correctly identifies the issue as a database query failure.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of describing architectural changes in a PR. The correct answer highlights that Sarah accurately explained her action: she implemented data validation. Options B and C are incorrect because they misrepresent the nature of the work (debugging vs. vague description). Option D is also wrong as it focuses on the database, not the user profile update.

Input Validation
System Integration

exercises.title: System Context Diagram Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Learn system context diagram vocabulary: system boundary, external actors, data flows, integration points, scope - the language for reading and presenting C4-level context diagrams in technical discussions.

questions.q: The architect points to the diagram and says: 'Everything inside this rectangle is within the system boundary.' What does 'system boundary' mean?
options: The physical network firewall that protects the servers
The line that separates the system we are building from everything outside it
The maximum number of concurrent users the system supports
The geographic boundary within which the system is deployed
questions.explanation: The system boundary is the conceptual line that defines what is 'inside' the system under discussion and what is 'outside'. In a C4 context diagram (Level 1), the system boundary separates your system from external actors (users, third-party services, other systems). It is fundamental for defining scope and responsibilities.

questions.q: During a diagram walkthrough, the engineer says: 'The external actors are the mobile app, the payment gateway, and the accounting system.' What is an 'external actor' in a system context diagram?
options: A security threat agent trying to attack the system
A person, organisation, or system outside the system boundary that interacts with it
A database table storing actor-related data
An internal service that handles authentication
questions.explanation: An external actor (also called an external entity or user) is anything outside the system boundary that sends data to or receives data from the system. External actors include human users, external APIs, third-party services, and other internal systems outside the scope of the diagram. They help define what the system must interface with.

questions.q: The architect says: 'This is out of scope for our system - it belongs to the payment provider.' What does 'out of scope' mean in this context?
options: The feature is planned for a future release
The functionality sits outside the system boundary and will be owned by another system or team
The feature is too complex to implement
The requirement has not yet been approved by the business
questions.explanation: 'Out of scope' means the functionality or concern is outside the system boundary - it belongs to an external actor or system. This is an important phrase in architecture discussions because it clarifies ownership and prevents teams from building functionality that is the responsibility of another system.

questions.q: A colleague says: 'Let's draw the data flows between our system and the external actors.' What do 'data flows' show in a system context diagram?
options: The speed of database queries within the system
The direction and nature of information exchanged between the system and its external actors
The internal data transformation steps in the ETL pipeline
The network bandwidth allocated to each service
questions.explanation: Data flows in a system context diagram show what information moves between the system and its external actors, and in which direction. For example, 'user sends login credentials → system returns authentication token'. Data flows help stakeholders understand the system's inputs, outputs, and dependencies at a high level.

questions.q: The architect explains: 'The integration points are the payment API, the SMS gateway, and the identity provider.' What is an 'integration point'?
options: A unit test that validates the connection between two modules
A place where the system connects to and exchanges data with an external system
An internal API endpoint exposed by a microservice
A database connection pool configuration
questions.explanation: An integration point is a specific connection where your system interfaces with an external system or service. Identifying integration points is critical in architecture work because each one represents a dependency, a potential failure mode, and a contract to maintain. Integration points appear as edges (lines) between your system and external actors in context diagrams.

questions.q: During a design review for the new e-commerce platform, Maria says: 'We need to show how our system interacts with the warehouse management system. Specifically, we'll represent the exchange of order details and shipment tracking information as a 'data flow' on the System Context Diagram.' What does she mean by 'data flow' in this scenario?
options: A. A physical cable connecting our servers to the warehouse.
B. The process of transferring data between two systems, typically represented visually with arrows indicating direction and volume.
C. A security protocol used to encrypt sensitive order information during transmission.
D. A scheduled maintenance task performed on the warehouse management system's database.
questions.explanation: Maria is referring to a 'data flow' as the visual representation of data being exchanged between systems - in this case, our e-commerce platform and the warehouse management system. The arrow indicates the direction of the transfer, and its thickness can represent the volume of data. This concept is crucial for understanding how components interact within the system boundary.

questions.q: Mark is presenting the System Context Diagram for a new mobile banking app. He explains: 'The customer uses the app to initiate a transfer. The app communicates with our core banking system via an API. Once the transfer is complete, we need to send a notification to the user's SMS gateway.' Mark then asks, 'What does it mean when we represent this communication path as an 'integration point' on the diagram?'
options: An integration point represents any physical connection between two systems.
An integration point is a specific interface or protocol used for exchanging data and commands between systems - in this case, the API call to our core banking system.
An integration point only applies to legacy systems that use serial communication.
An integration point is a security vulnerability that needs to be addressed during development.
questions.explanation: The correct answer highlights the key function of an integration point: it's a specific interface or protocol. Misconceptions often arise from thinking of integration points as purely physical connections (option A) or considering them only for older systems (option C). Option D is incorrect because integration points are designed to *facilitate* communication, not introduce vulnerabilities.

questions.q: During a demo of the new fraud detection system, Alex explains: 'The system receives alerts from our security monitoring platform and then automatically triggers investigations with our internal team. The security monitoring platform is considered an external actor in this diagram.' What does 'external actor' mean in this context?
options: A. An internal component of the same system that processes data.
B. A third-party service that provides information to the system, but isn't directly controlled by it.
C. A database table containing user account details.
D. The primary development team responsible for building the fraud detection system.
questions.explanation: An 'external actor' refers to anything outside of the system boundary - in this case, the security monitoring platform. exercises.title: System Design Interview Narration
exercises.subtitle: Practice the English vocabulary and sentence structures for narrating system design during interviews.

questions.q: An interviewer asks you to design a URL shortener. What is a good opening sentence?
options: I will use a database.
Let me start by clarifying the requirements - are we optimizing for read-heavy or write-heavy workloads, and what is the expected scale?
The URL shortener is simple.
I know how to do this.
questions.explanation: Good system design interviews begin with requirement clarification - scale, access patterns, and constraints before jumping to implementation.

questions.q: You are explaining a caching layer in your design. Which sentence is most technically precise?
options: We add a cache to make it fast.
We introduce a distributed cache (Redis) between the application tier and the database to reduce read latency for frequently accessed short URLs.
Caching is good.
The cache is a box.
questions.explanation: Precise system design language names the technology, its position in the architecture, and the problem it solves.

questions.q: How would you describe a trade-off between consistency and availability in your design?
options: We choose consistency or availability - it does not matter.
By choosing eventual consistency, we prioritize availability and partition tolerance, accepting that reads may return slightly stale data.
Consistency is always correct.
Availability is not important.
questions.explanation: The CAP theorem trade-off must be articulated explicitly: what is sacrificed and what is gained for the specific use case.

questions.q: You need to explain database sharding in your design. Which sentence is best?
options: Sharding means we split the data.
We horizontally partition the database by user ID, distributing load across multiple shards to scale beyond single-node capacity.
We add more columns.
Sharding is complex so we skip it.
questions.explanation: Sharding explanations should specify the sharding key, the partitioning strategy, and the scaling problem being solved.

questions.q: The interviewer asks: How would you handle 10x the current load? What is the best response?
options: We add more servers.
We would scale the stateless application tier horizontally, move to a read replica pattern for the database, and evaluate migrating hot data to a distributed cache.
We cannot handle 10x.
We rewrite everything.
questions.explanation: Scaling responses should address each bottleneck tier: application, database, and caching - with specific patterns for each.

questions.q: During a code review of a new microservice API endpoint, your teammate describes it as 'stateless and horizontally scalable.' You want to ensure you understand their intent fully. What's the most effective way to probe for clarification in this context? Specifically, what aspects are they prioritizing?
options: 'Can you elaborate on what constitutes a 'stateful' endpoint in this design?'
'So, you're saying we should implement session affinity for improved performance?'
'Could you walk me through the anticipated scaling challenges and how this architecture addresses them?'
'Does that mean we don't need to consider any potential bottlenecks related to network latency?'
questions.explanation: Option B is best because it directly challenges the teammate's use of 'stateless,' prompting a deeper discussion about their understanding of session management and its implications. Options A and D focus on misunderstandings or tangential concerns. Option C is too broad; while relevant, it doesn't specifically address the core term being discussed.

questions.q: During a code review of a new API endpoint designed to handle high volumes of requests, your senior engineer says, 'This needs to be highly available.' You want to ensure you fully understand the implications. Which response best demonstrates your understanding and prompts further discussion about specific strategies?
options: 'Okay, that makes sense. Can you elaborate on what measures we'll take to ensure high availability?'
'High availability is important, but I'm not sure how that relates to the API design itself.'
'Could you explain what you mean by 'high availability'? Are we talking about redundancy, failover mechanisms, or something else?'
'Sounds good! We should probably add some monitoring tools to track its availability.'
questions.explanation: The correct answer (option 2) acknowledges the importance of high availability while prompting a crucial clarification. It avoids assuming a specific implementation and directly asks for an explanation. Options A and B are too vague or don't actively seek understanding; option D focuses on a superficial monitoring aspect without addressing the core concern of resilience and fault tolerance, which 'high availability' inherently implies.

questions.q: During a design discussion for a new recommendation engine API, your team lead says, 'We need to ensure low latency for user requests.' You want to delve deeper into the specific technical choices being considered. Which of the following responses best demonstrates you're actively seeking more detail about their approach?
options: 'Sounds good! Just let me know when we've finalized the architecture.'
'Low latency is critical - can you elaborate on what strategies are being evaluated, such as caching or pre-computation?'
'That's a standard requirement. We should probably just stick with the existing PostgreSQL database.'
'Okay, so we're prioritizing speed? What metrics are we targeting for latency reduction?'
questions.explanation: Option 1 directly acknowledges the importance of low latency while requesting further clarification on the *methods* being considered. Options A and C demonstrate a passive acceptance without probing for specifics, while option B suggests a premature commitment to PostgreSQL which isn't necessarily relevant to the question of latency strategies.

questions.q: You're reviewing a PR for a new rate limiter. The developer states, 'We've implemented a token bucket algorithm to handle bursts.' You want to ensure you fully grasp the implications of this choice. Which response best demonstrates your understanding and prompts further discussion about potential considerations?
options: 'That's great! Can you elaborate on how frequently we should refill the bucket?'
'A token bucket sounds like a good solution for handling bursts. What's the bucket size, and how does it scale with increased traffic?'
'I understand. A token bucket is commonly used. Are there any specific performance metrics you're targeting related to burst handling?'
'Are we using Redis to store the tokens? That would likely be more efficient than a purely in-memory solution.'
questions.explanation: Option 1 is best because it directly probes for key details - bucket size and refill rate - which are crucial parameters of a token bucket algorithm. Options B and C simply acknowledge the technique without asking critical follow-up questions. Option D introduces an unrelated technology (Redis) that isn't central to understanding the core design choice.

questions.q: You're reviewing a pull request for a new API endpoint that processes user profile updates. Your teammate writes in the PR description: 'This service will use optimistic locking to prevent concurrent updates.' During the review, you want to ensure everyone's on the same page about this approach.
options: 'Optimistic locking sounds like a good way to avoid race conditions.'
'Can you elaborate on how optimistic locking will be implemented - specifically, what happens if a conflict occurs?'
'I understand optimistic locking; it's the standard approach for this type of operation.'
'We should probably consider pessimistic locking instead; it's generally more efficient.'
questions.explanation: The key here is to probe beyond a surface-level understanding. While 'optimistic locking sounds like a good way to avoid race conditions' is true in principle, it doesn't demonstrate an active attempt to understand the implementation details. Option B - asking about *how* it's implemented - pushes for clarification and ensures you grasp the practical mechanics of optimistic locking (e.g., rollbacks). Options A and C are accepting the statement without critical assessment, while option D introduces a potentially incorrect suggestion.
